opus-5.5.text:
I think part of it is that perception is so effortless for us that it becomes invisible. You open your eyes in the morning and the world is just *there*: the depth of the room, the cup on the table you can reach for, the person walking toward you whose intention you can already guess. None of that feels like work, so we don't think of it as intelligence. Language, on the other hand, feels like effort. We remember learning to read and write, we struggle to find the right words, and so we associate language with thinking itself.

But if you look at it through the lens of evolution, the story is almost reversed. Vision and the ability to act in a three-dimensional world go back more than five hundred million years. The Cambrian explosion is, in a sense, a story about eyes, about animals suddenly being able to see and therefore having to move, hunt, hide, and navigate. That's an enormous amount of evolutionary pressure shaping how a nervous system understands space, objects, physics, and cause and effect. Human language, by comparison, is a few hundred thousand years old at most. It's an extraordinary achievement, but it's built on top of this much deeper foundation of spatial understanding.

There's also a cultural reason. So much of what we celebrate as intellectual achievement, like literature, law, mathematics, and philosophy, gets recorded and transmitted in language. So we've developed a kind of bias where we equate intelligence with what can be written down. Meanwhile, the surgeon's hands, the carpenter's sense of how wood will behave, a toddler figuring out that a ball rolling behind the couch still exists: those are profound forms of intelligence, but they're harder to articulate, so we undervalue them.

And frankly, I think AI has reinforced this recently. Large language models have been so impressive that it's tempting to believe that if you master language, you've mastered intelligence. But language is a lossy, one-dimensional encoding of a world that is fundamentally three-dimensional, physical, and governed by its own rules. You can describe a cup falling off a table, but understanding *how* it falls, where the pieces go, and how to catch it requires a model of space and physics that words alone don't fully capture.

So for me, spatial intelligence isn't a side topic. It's the scaffolding that the rest of intelligence, including language, sits on. If we want machines that can truly understand, create, and act in the world alongside us, robots, creative tools, scientific discovery, then we have to take perception and spatial reasoning as seriously as we've taken language.

r001.rationale: The response says perception feels effortless and invisible, while language feels effortful because people remember learning to read and write and struggle to find words.

r002.rationale: It contrasts vision and spatial action developing over 500 million years with human language being only a few hundred thousand years old, and describes the evolutionary pressure shaping spatial understanding.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's because perception is so effortless for us that we don't even notice we're doing it. You wake up, you open your eyes, and the world is just there. You reach for your coffee cup and your hand lands on it. You walk through a doorway without bumping the frame. None of that feels like intelligence. It feels like being awake. But language is different. We remember learning to read. We struggle to write a good sentence. We can see the effort, so we assign it value.

But if you look at it from an evolutionary point of view, the picture flips completely. Animals have had vision for about 540 million years, since the Cambrian explosion. The arrival of eyes is arguably what triggered that explosion, because once you can see, you can hunt, you can hide, you can navigate, and the whole arms race of intelligence begins. Language, by comparison, is maybe a few hundred thousand years old. It's a very recent layer sitting on top of an extraordinarily deep foundation. Most of what the brain does, most of the cortex, is devoted to understanding and acting in a three-dimensional world. Language is wonderful, but it's the tip of the iceberg.

The other thing I'd say is that language is lossy in a way we rarely acknowledge. If I ask you to describe a room, you'll give me a few sentences, but the actual room contains an enormous amount of structure that words never capture. Where things are relative to each other, how far away the chair is, whether the glass is about to tip over, what will happen if I push this object. That spatial understanding, the ability to see, reason about, and interact with the physical world, is what I call spatial intelligence. It's how we build, how we make things, how we take care of each other. And it predates words entirely.

I also think the recent success of large language models reinforced the bias. We saw machines become fluent, and because fluency is what we associate with being smart, it was easy to feel like the problem was mostly solved. But fluency about the world is not the same as understanding the world. A model can describe what a cup is and still have no idea how to grasp one. So part of why I keep talking about this is that I think the next big step for AI, and honestly for our understanding of ourselves, is to take perception and space as seriously as we've taken language.

r001.rationale: It says perception feels effortless and goes unnoticed, while people remember the effort of learning to read and writing, so they assign language more value.

r002.rationale: It contrasts vision dating back about 540 million years and spatial abilities as a deep foundation with language as a recent development only a few hundred thousand years old.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that perception feels effortless to us. You open your eyes, and the world is just there. You recognize a face, you reach for a cup, you walk through a crowded room. You don’t consciously experience the complexity of those tasks, so it’s easy to overlook how much intelligence they require.

Language is different. We’re very aware of the effort involved in finding the right words, constructing an argument, or learning a new language. So we tend to associate intelligence with those things that feel intellectually demanding.

But consider what it takes to pick up that cup. You need to understand its shape, where it is relative to your body, how to grasp it, and what will happen when you move it. Perception and action are tightly connected. Spatial intelligence is about that connection—understanding a world you can interact with, not just describe.

Language is enormously important. But so much of our intelligence operates before we say a single word.

r001.rationale: It says people are consciously aware of the effort involved in finding words, constructing arguments, and learning languages, unlike the effortless-feeling experience of perception.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention evolution or compare how long it has optimized perception and spatial intelligence versus language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that perception feels effortless to us. You open your eyes and you see a room. You recognize the objects, understand where things are, and know how to move through it. You don’t consciously calculate any of that, so it’s easy to overlook how much intelligence it requires.

Language is much more explicit. We spend years learning to read and write, and we associate articulate speech with sophisticated thought. But think about the intelligence involved in picking up a cup: understanding its shape, its position, how your hand should approach it, what might happen if you tip it. There’s a tremendous amount of understanding beneath that simple action.

Spatial intelligence connects perception to action. It’s not just recognizing what’s in an image; it’s understanding a world you can interact with. Because we live with that ability every moment, we tend to take it for granted.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts effortless perception with the years of conscious effort spent learning language, presenting that difference as a reason perception is overlooked.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention evolution or compare how long evolution has optimized perception and spatial intelligence versus language.
